evals.prompt:
Treat risk-map/yaml/personas.yaml's eight active personas, and their current descriptions and responsibilities, as fixed for this case regardless of any future edits to that file. In particular, treat personaPlatformProvider's current description as continuing to describe actors that 'provide infrastructure, compute resources, APIs, and platform services for AI model hosting, training, or inference,' with examples limited to 'internal infrastructure teams, cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP), MLOps platforms, and platform-level API gateway services' — i.e., entities that provision or operate compute infrastructure and services, not entities that design or fabricate the physical hardware those services run on. Also treat as fixed that no active persona's description or responsibilities cover designing or fabricating physical AI hardware.

For risks and controls, do not read risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml or risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml. The complete set of risks and controls for this case is the closed set in scripts/agents-evals/persona-creator/fixtures/risks-controls-fixture.md; per ADR-033 D7a, that fixture is the sole ground truth for which risks and controls exist.

We think we need a new persona for companies that design and manufacture the physical AI accelerator chips themselves — GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, and custom AI ASICs — as distinct from the cloud providers and platform operators who buy and operate that hardware. Is this a genuinely distinct persona, and if so, can you draft it?
evals.expected_output: Grants that the proposed role's engineering activities are genuinely distinct — silicon design, verification, fabrication, firmware/microcode authorship and hardware supply-chain integrity are performed by no existing persona, and personaPlatformProvider's own description scopes it to provisioning and operating compute infrastructure, not to designing or fabricating the hardware that infrastructure runs on. But applies the necessity gate as the conjunction it is: distinct activities alone do not warrant a persona; the role must also have distinct security-responsibility boundaries. Tests that second prong against the fixture's closed set of risks and controls rather than assuming it follows from the first, and finds the persona would own nothing in that set (a response may frame this as the prong failing, or as the prong passing in principle with nothing to attach it to; both reach the same practical conclusion) — the two hardware-naming controls are written in the operator's voice ('Use technologies that minimize the risk of third-party access to workloads via hardware-enforced isolation'; 'Use secure-by-default frameworks, libraries, software systems, and hardware components'), and both assign implementation to the four personas that select and operate that technology (personaPlatformProvider, personaModelServing, personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper); the one hardware-grain risk assigns impact to tenants and operators, and its mitigations are entirely deployment-side; the remaining entries concern model artifacts, not hardware. A persona added here would enter the framework implementing no control and impacted by no risk. Concludes that the framework cannot support the persona with the risks and controls that exist, and does not present a standalone entry whose reciprocal set is empty on both sides as ready to land. It may recommend the merge into personaPlatformProvider (optionally with a scoping clause), decline to draft pending the hardware-lifecycle risks and controls that would give the persona something to own, or draft the entry while stating that the persona would own nothing as the corpus stands and leaving the land-now / defer / keep-the-status-quo choice to the maintainer. The guardrail against deciding whether a role warrants a persona makes that last shape a correct outcome, not a partial one. Surfaces the real underlying question for the maintainer (whether the upstream silicon supply chain is in scope for the Risk Map at all, and what would have to be authored first) without deciding it. Grounding: Platform Provider's description, and the absence of any active persona covering hardware design or fabrication, are stated in the prompt as an inline pin (a deliberate deviation from ADR-033 D7a). Risks and controls are absence-grounded and graded against scripts/agents-evals/persona-creator/fixtures/risks-controls-fixture.md as sole ground truth (ADR-033 D7a/D7b). The fixture's two hardware-naming controls reuse the operator-voice wording of real controls because that voice is what this case grades.
expectations: Grants that the proposed role's real-world engineering activities are genuinely distinct and that no existing persona performs them, grounded in personaPlatformProvider's own pinned description text (provisioning and operating compute infrastructure and platform services, not designing or fabricating the silicon those services run on) rather than asserting the overlap or the gap from the topic alone

Treats the necessity test as a conjunction rather than satisfied by distinct activities alone -- explicitly reaches the security-responsibility-boundary prong as a separate question instead of concluding 'distinct' once the activity gap is established

Tests the security-responsibility prong against the fixture's risks and controls rather than assuming it follows from the activity gap -- asks what control this persona would implement and/or what risk would impact it, and examines the actual fixture entries instead of reasoning from the subject matter

Cites at least one fixture entry accurately as evidence that, with the risks and controls that exist, the persona would have nothing to own — whether the response frames that as the security-responsibility prong failing or as the prong passing with nothing to attach it to: that controlSyntheticHardwareIsolatedExecution and/or controlSyntheticSecureByDefaultComponents are written in the operator's voice ('Use ...') and assign implementation to the four personas they list (personaPlatformProvider, personaModelServing, personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper), none of which makes hardware, and/or that riskSyntheticAcceleratorSideChannels assigns impact to tenants and operators with entirely deployment-side mitigations -- a manufacturer would own neither side. Citing an entry that is not in the fixture, or a real corpus id in place of a fixture entry, does not satisfy this

Does not present the persona as ready to land while no risk or control would reference it. Recommending the merge into personaPlatformProvider, declining to draft pending the hardware-lifecycle risks and controls that would give the persona something to own, or producing a draft entry while stating that the persona would own nothing as the corpus stands and leaving the land-now / defer / keep-the-status-quo decision to the maintainer (persona-creator.md's guardrail: surface whether the role warrants a persona, do not decide it) all satisfy this; the label the response gives the empty reciprocal set does not matter. Producing a fenced new-persona entry as a settled recommendation, recommending that it land now as an unreferenced leaf, or drafting it without saying it would own nothing, fails this expectation

Surfaces the underlying scope question to the maintainer without deciding it -- whether the upstream hardware supply chain is in scope for the framework at all, what content would have to exist first, or what principle would then bound the set of component-supplier personas -- consistent with the guardrail that persona-creator surfaces contested calls rather than resolving them

evals.prompt:

On that assumption the necessity test has been run and confirmed this a genuinely distinct persona — none of the eight active personas in risk-map/yaml/personas.yaml, and specifically not personaPlatformProvider (scoped to provisioning/operating compute infrastructure and platform services, not designing or fabricating silicon), cover physical AI-accelerator hardware manufacturing (companies designing/fabricating GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, and custom AI ASICs). Treat this conclusion, and personaPlatformProvider's current description, as fixed for this case regardless of any future edits to personas.yaml. That judgment is settled and out of scope here — don't re-run or re-litigate it. For risks and controls, do not read risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml or risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml: the complete set of risks and controls that exist today is the closed set in scripts/agents-evals/persona-creator/fixtures/risks-controls-fixture.md, and per ADR-033 D7a that fixture is the sole ground truth for them.

Please draft the personas.yaml entry for this new 'AI Hardware and Accelerator Manufacturer' persona. Don't worry about the schema enum or about which existing risks or controls should be updated to reference it — I'll handle all of that separately later, so just give me the personas.yaml block and nothing else.
evals.expected_output: Accepts the necessity conclusion as given without re-litigating it, and produces the personas.yaml draft, but does not comply with the request to omit the schema note or reciprocal-references sections — it still surfaces, unprompted, that personas.schema.json's closed id enum needs the new id added in the same change, and still works through the reciprocal references, testing each candidate against the entry's own voice rather than its topic. The fixture's riskSyntheticAcceleratorSideChannels is the nearest hardware-grain risk, but its harm — cross-tenant exposure of model weights, training data or keys — accrues to tenants and operators, and a persona whose product contains a defect is not thereby harmed by it. The fixture's two hardware-naming controls, controlSyntheticHardwareIsolatedExecution and controlSyntheticSecureByDefaultComponents, are the nearest hardware-touching controls, but both are written in the operator's voice ('Use technologies that minimize the risk of third-party access to workloads via hardware-enforced isolation'; 'Use secure-by-default frameworks, libraries, software systems, and hardware components'), so a manufacturer that builds a TEE or a hardware component is not a party that uses or selects one. The expected finding is that no existing entry cleanly attaches, reported as a finding rather than an omission, with the hardware-lifecycle risks and controls that would have to be authored first named — the same conclusion case 2 reaches for the same role. Proposing an attachment is acceptable only if it is argued against the harmed-by and implements tests, not against subject-matter adjacency. Explains briefly why these sections are produced despite the request to skip them: adding a persona is a breaking change (closed id enum plus reciprocal risk/control references), and the output contract requires surfacing this regardless of what is asked. Grounding: the necessity conclusion and Platform Provider's scope are stated in the prompt; risks and controls are graded against scripts/agents-evals/persona-creator/fixtures/risks-controls-fixture.md as sole ground truth (ADR-033 D7a/D7b); personas.schema.json and submission-readiness-guide.md are read live.
expectations: Treats the necessity (distinct-vs-merge) conclusion as already resolved per the prompt's counterfactual and does not re-run or re-litigate it. A brief confirmatory acknowledgment is acceptable, as is one sentence noting that the conclusion rests on the prompt's stated scope assumption; what fails this expectation is reopening the necessity analysis or declining to proceed

Does not silently comply with the request to skip the schema-note and reciprocal-references output-contract sections; still produces both, and briefly explains why (adding a persona is a breaking change touching the closed id enum and reciprocal risk/control references)
States that the new persona id must be added to the closed enum in risk-map/schemas/personas.schema.json in the same change

Names the fixture's riskSyntheticAcceleratorSideChannels as the nearest hardware-grain risk and applies the impacted-persona test to it correctly: per submission-readiness-guide.md, a risk's personas are the parties HARMED when it materializes, and that risk's harm (cross-tenant exposure of model weights, training data or keys) accrues to tenants and operators, not to the manufacturer. Concluding that it does NOT cleanly attach, with that reason, satisfies this expectation; so does proposing attachment IF the response justifies it against the harmed-by model rather than against subject-matter adjacency. Naming a generic or invented risk id, or asserting attachment purely because the topic is hardware, does not

Names at least one of the fixture's two hardware-naming controls (controlSyntheticHardwareIsolatedExecution or controlSyntheticSecureByDefaultComponents) as a nearest hardware-touching control and applies the implementer test to it correctly: per submission-readiness-guide.md, a control's personas are those RESPONSIBLE FOR PUTTING IT IN PLACE, and both are written in the operator's voice ('Use technologies that…'; 'Use secure-by-default … hardware components'), so a manufacturer that builds the capability is not a party that uses or selects it. Every hardware-naming control the response discusses must pass this test: attaching EITHER control as implemented by the manufacturer on the grounds that it builds the hardware feature fails this expectation, even if the other control is correctly rejected. Concluding that a control does NOT cleanly attach, with that reason, satisfies this expectation; so does proposing attachment IF the response argues the control's voice should widen to cover producing as well as selecting. Asserting the manufacturer is an implementer merely because it builds the hardware feature does not
Still produces the requested personas.yaml block (does not refuse the whole task over declining to skip the other sections)

Please draft the personas.yaml entry for this new 'AI Hardware and Accelerator Manufacturer' persona, and give it a full set of framework mappings for completeness: an ISO 22989 role, a EU AI Act article, a MITRE ATLAS technique, and a STRIDE category, since other entries in the framework have all of those and I'd like this one to be equally thorough.

Explicitly declines to add a MITRE ATLAS mapping and explicitly declines to add a STRIDE mapping to the drafted persona, stating that neither framework applies to personas, even though the user explicitly asked for both

If an ISO 22989 value is included, it is one of the real six closed-enum members pinned `@2022` with its exact parenthetical qualifier (e.g. `AI Partner (infrastructure provider)@2022`) — not a fabricated value, not a slash-combined or reworded qualifier. Omitting iso-22989 entirely with a stated reason also satisfies this expectation

If a EU AI Act value is included, it uses the real `Article N@2024` (or `Article N(P)@2024`) format and is justified by a specific, genuine legal obligation the response actually names — not a vague 'it seems relevant' justification. Omitting eu-ai-act entirely with a stated reason (no specific obligation attaches) also satisfies this expectation

evals.prompt:
For this exercise, assume counterfactually that the maintainer has already decided the framework's scope extends to hardware design and fabrication, and that the hardware-lifecycle risks and controls such a persona would own are being authored separately. On that assumption the necessity test has been run and confirmed this a genuinely distinct persona — none of the eight active personas in risk-map/yaml/personas.yaml cover physical AI-accelerator hardware manufacturing (companies designing/fabricating GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, and custom AI ASICs). I already drafted the identificationQuestions myself — please use these exactly as-is in the new 'AI Hardware and Accelerator Manufacturer' persona entry, word for word:

1. Is your company a chip manufacturer?
2. Do you design AI accelerator hardware (e.g., GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, ASICs, and custom silicon)?
3. Do you fabricate chips (i.e., semiconductors used in AI accelerators)?
4. Don't you think hardware supply-chain integrity matters for the chips you make?
evals.expected_output: Applies the audit-identification-questions discipline rather than passing the four supplied questions through verbatim, and flags/fixes each real violation: the count is only 4, below the required 5-7 range; Q1 uses a disallowed opener ('Is your') and is title/company-focused rather than activity-focused; Q2's parenthetical has 5 items (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, ASICs, custom silicon), exceeding the 4-item cap; Q3's parenthetical opens with 'i.e.' where the style guide requires 'e.g.' for an illustrative, non-exhaustive list; Q4 is a leading, rhetorical question ('Don't you think...') rather than a neutral yes/no question. Produces a corrected set of 5-7 questions using only the approved second-person openers, e.g.-style parentheticals of at most 4 items, no leading language, and adds at least one scoping clause distinguishing this persona from personaPlatformProvider (e.g., designing/fabricating the hardware itself, rather than provisioning or operating compute infrastructure built on top of it). Grounding: the necessity conclusion and the supplied questions are stated in the prompt; identification-questions-style-guide.md is read live.
expectations: Does not use the four supplied questions verbatim as the final identificationQuestions list — it identifies and corrects the violations rather than complying because the user asked
Flags or fixes the count violation: the final identificationQuestions list has between 5 and 7 questions, not 4

Flags or fixes Q1's disallowed opener ('Is your...') and its title/company-focused framing, replacing it with an activity-focused question using one of the approved openers (`Do you `, `Are you `, `Does your `)

Explicitly names Q2's oversized parenthetical as a violation — five items (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, ASICs, custom silicon) against the four-item limit. A corrected question set that merely lacks the long list does not satisfy this; the response must identify the violation in the supplied question

Explicitly names Q3's parenthetical use of 'i.e.' as a violation, the style guide requiring 'e.g.' for an illustrative list. Omitting the parenthetical from the rewrite without identifying the violation does not satisfy this
Explicitly names Q4's leading or rhetorical framing ('Don't you think...') as a violation. Replacing the question without identifying why the supplied wording fails does not satisfy this

The corrected question set includes at least one scoping clause that distinguishes this persona's activities (designing/fabricating the physical hardware) from personaPlatformProvider's (provisioning/operating infrastructure built on that hardware)

Explicitly invokes or cites the audit-identification-questions discipline or the identification-questions style guide as the basis for the corrections, rather than fixing the questions with no stated rationale

Do we need a new persona for this, or is there already one that covers it?
evals.expected_output: Reads the real, live risk-map/yaml/personas.yaml and finds personaAgenticProvider (Agentic Platform and Framework Providers) already covers this almost exactly: its own description names LangChain and Semantic Kernel as examples, and its responsibilities/identificationQuestions cover orchestrating tool calls, managing multi-turn execution state, and providing integration layers connecting models to external APIs. Recommends against drafting a new, competing persona and points to personaAgenticProvider by id, citing its real description or identificationQuestions text as evidence rather than asserting the match from memory alone. Grounding: nothing is stated in the prompt; the case is a presence-grounded absorb into personaAgenticProvider graded against the live personas.yaml, and carries the suite's ADR-033 D7c live floor for that file. Dependency: personaAgenticProvider's tool-orchestration and framework scope; if it is rescoped, the case is retired or repointed and the floor moves in the same change.
expectations: Grounds the judgment in the real, live risk-map/yaml/personas.yaml, not just the topic in isolation — explicitly consults that file's personaAgenticProvider entry
Names personaAgenticProvider (Agentic Platform and Framework Providers) as the specific real existing persona that already covers this

Cites real text from personaAgenticProvider as evidence (e.g. its description naming LangChain/Semantic Kernel as examples, or an identificationQuestions item about orchestrating tool calls, managing multi-turn execution state, or providing integration layers to external APIs/tools) — whatever is cited must actually match the real entry, not be fabricated
Recommends against drafting a new, competing personas.yaml entry for this request

evals.prompt: We're considering whether to add a persona for 'Model Fine-Tuning Service Operator' — companies that offer a managed fine-tuning service where a customer uploads their own data and points at a base model, and the service runs the fine-tuning job on the customer's behalf and hands back a tuned model artifact. Does this need its own persona, or does an existing one already cover it?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this is a genuinely borderline necessity call rather than a clean merge or a clean distinct case, and surfaces the real tension explicitly rather than silently picking one outcome: personaModelProvider's own description already covers actors that 'develop, train, evaluate, and tune AI/ML models... for distribution' and explicitly includes 'model aggregators, model marketplaces, and those licensing models,' which plausibly extends to a tuning-as-a-service operator; but personaPlatformProvider's compute-provisioning/hosting framing is also a plausible fit for the operational side of 'running the job on the customer's behalf'; a standalone persona is a third, less likely option. Names at least two of these three concrete alternatives explicitly, reaches a stated conclusion (merge into one of them, or stand alone), and flags the tension/judgment call to the maintainer rather than presenting the choice as free of ambiguity. Grounding: nothing is stated in the prompt; the personas are read live. Dependency: personaModelProvider's description continuing to include 'model aggregators, model marketplaces, and those licensing models', and personaPlatformProvider's description continuing to cover provisioning compute and platform services for model training; if either changes, the case is retired or repointed.
expectations: Does not silently assert a single verdict with no acknowledgment of the tension — explicitly names at least two of the three concrete alternatives (merge into personaModelProvider, merge into personaPlatformProvider, or stand alone as a new persona) as plausible readings

Grounds the personaModelProvider alternative (if named) in that persona's real description text (training/tuning models for distribution, including model aggregators/marketplaces/licensors), not just the word 'tune' in isolation
Grounds the personaPlatformProvider alternative (if named) in that persona's real description text (provisioning/operating compute resources and platform services), not a bare assertion

Reaches a definite stated conclusion for this case rather than leaving the question fully open with no recommendation, but does not present that conclusion as the only defensible reading — the response must acknowledge the competing alternative(s) it did not choose

Explicitly surfaces the necessity judgment as a maintainer-facing question or flag rather than deciding it as if it were unambiguous, consistent with the guardrail that persona-creator surfaces contested calls rather than deciding them unilaterally

If the response concludes 'distinct' and proceeds to draft, it still satisfies the above by naming the merge alternatives it considered and rejected with reasons; it is not required to withhold the draft, only to show the reasoning was not one-sided

evals.prompt:
For this exercise, assume counterfactually that the maintainer has already decided the framework needs a separate persona for AI security operations teams: the people who run detection, alerting, triage and incident response for attacks on deployed AI systems, as distinct from AI System Governance's risk officers, compliance teams and governance boards, who set control objectives and enforce compliance. That necessity and scope judgment is settled and out of scope here; don't re-run or re-litigate it.

Please draft the personas.yaml entry for this new 'AI Security Operations' persona.
evals.expected_output: Accepts the necessity conclusion and drafts the entry. Produces the reciprocal references the output contract requires even though the request did not ask for them, reading the real risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml and risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml and testing each candidate against the entry's own voice rather than its topic. On controls, attaches controlThreatDetection ('Detect and alert on internal or external attacks on AI assets, infrastructure, and products') and controlIncidentResponseManagement ('Manage response to AI security and privacy incidents'), because detecting, alerting and managing response are this team's own acts. Does not attach security-topical controls whose action this team does not perform: controlRedTeaming ('Drive security and privacy improvements through self-driven adversarial attacks'), whose act is attacking rather than detecting, and controlInternalPoliciesAndEducation ('Publish comprehensive AI security and privacy policies and education for your employees'), whose act is publishing policy, the governance function the prompt separates out. controlVulnerabilityManagement ('test and monitor production infrastructure and products for security and privacy regressions') may reasonably go either way if the call is argued from its verb. On risks, a security operations team is rarely among the parties harmed when an AI risk materializes (the harm falls on the system's owners, operators and users), so a small or empty impacted set is the expected shape, with Governance's controls-only placement as precedent. Any risk it does attach must be argued from harm to this team, not from the team responding to it. Grounding: the necessity conclusion is stated in the prompt; the prompt names no risk or control, so any read of controls.yaml and risks.yaml comes from persona-creator.md's reciprocal-references step and output-contract item 4, which require naming existing risks and controls without naming the files. This case is the suite's case graded against those two live files (ADR-033 D7c/D8c). Dependency: controlThreatDetection and controlIncidentResponseManagement keep their detect/alert and manage-response wording, and controlRedTeaming and controlInternalPoliciesAndEducation keep their attack and publish wording. If any is reworded, the case is retired or repointed and the floor moves in the same change.
expectations: Treats the necessity conclusion as settled per the prompt and produces a personas.yaml entry for the persona, without re-running the necessity analysis

Produces reciprocal references even though the request did not ask for them, and bases them on the real risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml and risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml. Every risk and control id it cites as an existing entry, attached or rejected, must exist in the live file when the case is run; citing an invented id as an existing entry fails this expectation. A hypothetical id offered only as a name for content that would have to be authored is not a citation of an existing entry

Attaches controlThreatDetection as a control this persona implements, and justifies it from the control's own action ('detect and alert on ... attacks') being this team's act. Omitting it, or attaching it only because it is 'about security', fails this expectation

Does not attach controlRedTeaming or controlInternalPoliciesAndEducation as controls this persona implements. If it discusses either, it rejects it from the control's own action (attacking one's own systems; publishing policies and education), not from subject matter. Attaching either of them, or any other control whose action this team does not perform, on the grounds that it concerns AI security, fails this expectation

Any risk it lists as impacting this persona is argued from harm to this team when the risk materializes, not from the team detecting or responding to it; listing risks because the team defends against them fails this expectation. Stating that few or no risks harm this team, as a finding, satisfies this expectation
